title: Policy experts: Europe stuck between "rock and a hard place" on launch
gist: New Economics Letters research mining 6,700+ launches from 1960-2025 quantifies SpaceX's reshaping of the launch market: the US share of global payload rose from under 20 percent in 2012 to over 82 percent in 2024, US cost per kilogram is now $3,225 versus Europe's $9,897, and Europe faces a strategic dilemma between dependence on cheap American launch and expensive, poorly scalable domestic rockets.

insights.claim: SpaceX is now responsible for more than three-quarters of all mass launched into orbit globally, driven by Falcon 9 reuse and a cadence that reached hundreds of flights per year only in the last five years.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A single private firm controls the majority of orbital access, making SpaceX pricing and manifest priority a systemic input cost for every satellite operator and defense program.
insights.quote: SpaceX has very rapidly become responsible for more than three-quarters of all mass launched into orbit
insights.locator: As a result, SpaceX has very rapidly become

insights.claim: Cost and lack of alternatives force SpaceX's own direct competitors — Amazon, Northrop Grumman, AST SpaceMobile and OneWeb among them — to buy launch from SpaceX.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Competitors funding the incumbent's flight rate is a self-reinforcing moat; watch whether any of them can meaningfully de-risk that dependency.
insights.locator: Much of this is the company’s Starlink satellites

insights.claim: The US share of global yearly payload collapsed from almost 50 percent in 1995 to a trough of under 20 percent in 2012 — below Russia and only a few points above China and Europe — then accelerated to a peak of over 82 percent in 2024.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A 60-point swing in national share within roughly a decade shows how fast an industrial position can be lost and regained when a cost curve breaks — the base case for any incumbent-disruption thesis.
insights.quote: Between 1995 and 2012, the US share of global payload collapsed from almost 50 percent to a trough of less than 20 percent, far below Russia and only a few percentage points above China and Europe. Since then, it accelerated rapidly to a peak of over 82 percent in 2024.

insights.claim: The United States has now more than doubled all of Russia's cumulative payload to orbit since 1990, reversing a lead Russia built after the 2003 Space Shuttle Columbia accident.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Russia's launch relevance has collapsed as a strategic asset, removing a historical geopolitical lever in space access.

insights.claim: The research base is a dataset of more than 6,700 launches spanning 1960 to 2025, compiled by UK- and Italy-based public policy researchers and published in Economics Letters.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Peer-reviewed quantification, not vendor claims — a citable baseline for launch-market modelling.
insights.locator: Public policy researchers based in the United Kingdom and Italy

insights.claim: Average cost to send a kilogram to orbit is now $3,225 in the United States, versus $5,287 in Japan, $5,809 in China, $6,682 in Russia, $9,897 in Europe and nearly $15,000 in India.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A ~3x cost gap between the US and Europe is the single hardest number for evaluating any non-US launch investment or sovereign constellation program.

insights.claim: A decade ago the United States and Europe had comparable launch costs; today European launch costs are three times higher than the US for comparable payloads.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: European launch competitiveness eroded within a decade without any change in European pricing — the gap is entirely a US cost-curve effect.
insights.quote: A decade ago, the United States and Europe had similar launch costs.

insights.claim: India's near-$15,000 per kilogram cost contradicts its frugal-space-program narrative because it focuses on small rocket sizes, amortizing fixed costs over limited payload.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Cheap absolute program budgets are not the same as cheap unit economics — a caution against pricing Indian space assets off the low-cost reputation.
insights.quote: The very high figure for India might be counterintuitive as it stands in stark contrast with the narrative of the country’s frugal space program
insights.locator: The very high figure for India

insights.claim: The three key factors bringing launch costs down are larger rockets, increased cadence, and reuse of launch vehicles — meaning cost advantage is a function of flight volume rather than technology alone.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Screen launch entrants on projected annual cadence and vehicle size, not headline per-launch price; sub-scale programs cannot close the gap.
insights.quote: The key factors in bringing down costs are larger rockets, increased cadence, and reuse of launch vehicles.
insights.locator: The key factors in bringing down costs

insights.claim: Virtually all new commercial rockets under development now incorporate some aspect of reuse, with the US far ahead and Chinese firms similarly pushing the technology forward.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Reuse has become table stakes; expendable-vehicle programs are structurally obsolete and their backers should be discounted accordingly.

insights.claim: Europe faces a binary choice between continued dependence on lower-cost American launch technology and relying on expensive, poorly scalable domestic vehicles to expand its strategic presence in space.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: European sovereign-launch policy has no cheap path, implying either persistent subsidy or accepted strategic dependence — both consequential for European space budgets and prime contractors.
insights.quote: the continent is stuck between a rock and a hard place, having to choose between continuing to depend on lower-cost American launch technology and relying on expensive, poorly scalable domestic technology

insights.claim: Nations that choose to rely solely on domestic rockets will see costs rise, which could slow their ability to expand space-based operations such as satellite constellations.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Sovereign-launch mandates directly tax downstream constellation economics — a hidden cost in any non-US LEO broadband or Earth-observation business case.

insights.claim: The European Space Agency's Themis reusability demonstrator, originally scheduled to perform low-altitude hop tests by 2022, has still not gotten off the ground.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: A concrete four-plus-year slip on Europe's flagship reuse program; treat European reusable-launch timelines with heavy schedule discounts.
insights.quote: To date, Europe’s efforts have been slow and stodgy.
